questions.text: When must an architect recuse themselves from an engagement due to conflict of interest, rather than proceeding with disclosure and consent?

options.text: An architect should never recuse; disclosure and consent always suffice, as long as all parties are informed and agree
When the conflicts are irreconcilable, confidential information cannot be unlearned, or the situation creates fundamental values conflict compromising professional integrity
Recusal is only required for family relationships, which are considered inherently biased and unmanageable
An architect must recuse from any engagement involving a competing interest, even if disclosure and consent are obtained

rationale.a: Some conflicts are so fundamental that disclosure and consent cannot adequately protect the client.
rationale.c: Family relationships can sometimes be managed through disclosure; irreconcilable conflicts require recusal.
rationale.d: Overstates the requirement; many competing interests are manageable through disclosure and consent.
rationale.correct: Disclosure and consent cannot cure irreconcilable conflicts, confidentiality breaches, or situations where fundamental professional integrity is compromised; recusal is then required.
rationale.takeaway: Recusal is required when conflicts are fundamentally irreconcilable, not merely when a competing interest exists.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Irreconcilable Conflicts & Recusal

questions.text: An architect receives a commission from a mechanical systems supplier whenever the architect specifies that supplier's equipment. The architect does not disclose this arrangement to clients. What is the primary ethical problem?

options.text: The supplier's equipment is lower quality than alternatives, potentially compromising project standards
The commission creates financial incentive that may bias the architect's judgment away from client's best interests, compromising objectivity without disclosure
Commission arrangements are never acceptable under any circumstances, as they inherently conflict with professional ethics
The architect must obtain written permission from the supplier before receiving the commission, which is not a standard practice

rationale.a: Quality is not the issue; the problem is the hidden financial incentive affecting the recommendation.
rationale.c: Commissions are permissible if disclosed and the client consents; the issue is non-disclosure.
rationale.d: Supplier permission is irrelevant; the architect must disclose to the client, who holds the decision-making power.
rationale.correct: Undisclosed supplier commissions create financial conflicts because the architect's compensation increases with the supplier's selection, biasing judgment without client knowledge.
rationale.takeaway: Undisclosed supplier commissions are prohibited because the financial incentive biases recommendation away from client benefit.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Conflict of Interest & Disclosure

questions.text: What must happen after an architect identifies and discloses a conflict of interest to the client?

options.text: The architect must immediately withdraw from the engagement, regardless of the client's wishes or any potential mitigation measures
The client must accept the conflict without any right to decline or impose conditions, even if the conflict affects project outcomes
The architect must obtain the client's informed, written consent before proceeding, with the client's clear right to decline or impose mitigation conditions
Disclosure is sufficient; no further client action is required, and the project can proceed without any changes

rationale.a: Withdrawal is not always required; many conflicts can be managed through disclosure and consent.
rationale.b: The client has autonomy to accept, decline, or impose conditions after full disclosure.
rationale.d: Disclosure without consent is ethically insufficient; the client must affirmatively agree to proceed.
rationale.correct: Disclosure alone is insufficient; the architect must obtain written informed consent from the client, who has the right to decline proceeding or require mitigation steps.
rationale.takeaway: After disclosure, the architect must obtain the client's written informed consent; the client must have the right to decline or impose conditions.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Informed Consent & Client Autonomy

questions.text: An architect's cousin is the City Engineer overseeing a municipal project for which the architect was selected through competitive bidding. The architect does not disclose the family relationship. What is the consequence?

options.text: Family relationships automatically invalidate project awards, leading to the immediate cancellation of the contract
The non-disclosed family relationship violates the duty of honesty; both the architect's client and the City Engineer's employer are entitled to know the relationship exists
The architect's bias is unimportant; only the City Engineer has a conflict, as the architect's role is purely technical
Disclosure is only required if the cousin helps evaluate the architect's work, ensuring that the evaluation process remains impartial

rationale.a: Disclosure cures the conflict in most cases; relationships don't automatically invalidate awards.
rationale.c: Appearance of favoritism affects the architect's credibility with the client, regardless of actual bias.
rationale.d: The relationship itself is the conflict; the cousin's role in evaluation is secondary.
rationale.correct: Non-disclosed family relationships violate honesty obligations; both the architect's client and public officials deserve to know the relationship.
rationale.takeaway: Family relationships with public officials overseeing your work must be disclosed to maintain public trust and professional integrity.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Honesty & Public Trust

questions.text: An architect agrees to represent two clients with materially opposed interests on the same project without disclosing the dual representation to either client. What is the ethical violation?

options.text: Simultaneous representation of two clients is inherently prohibited, as it creates unavoidable conflicts of interest
The non-disclosed dual representation violates the duty of exclusive loyalty and honesty; both clients' interests are compromised without their knowledge
Dual representation requires the architect to withdraw only from the smaller project, ensuring no conflict of interest remains
The architect's conflict of interest is cured by disclosure to only one of the clients, assuming the other client remains unaware

rationale.a: Dual representation is permissible with disclosure and consent; the issue is lack of disclosure.
rationale.c: Withdrawal from one client does not solve the other client's undisclosed conflict.
rationale.d: Both clients must be informed; disclosing to one while hiding from the other compounds the violation.
rationale.correct: Undisclosed dual representation violates exclusivity and candor; both clients deserve to know their interests may be divided and to consent or decline.
rationale.takeaway: Dual representation with opposed interests is prohibited unless both clients are fully informed and consent in writing.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Exclusive Loyalty & Dual Representation

questions.text: What is the objective standard for determining whether a conflict of interest exists?

options.text: The architect's subjective belief about whether they can remain impartial, which may not align with external perceptions
Whether a competing interest could reasonably appear to compromise objectivity, regardless of the architect's belief in their impartiality
Whether the architect actually receives financial benefit, which is often the most direct indicator of a conflict
Whether the client explicitly asks about potential conflicts, indicating awareness and concern about impartiality

rationale.a: Misunderstands the standard; the architect's subjective belief is irrelevant—the test is objective appearance of impropriety.
rationale.c: Actual financial benefit is not the only trigger; even the appearance of potential benefit can create a conflict.
rationale.d: Client inquiry is not required; the architect has a duty to recognize and disclose conflicts proactively.
rationale.correct: Conflicts are determined objectively—whether a reasonable third party would view the competing interest as compromising objectivity, not by the architect's subjective belief in their own impartiality.
rationale.takeaway: Conflicts of interest are determined objectively; a reasonable appearance of impropriety triggers disclosure, regardless of the architect's subjective confidence.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Professional Conduct & Ethics

questions.text: An architect is involved in litigation as an expert witness defending another architect. The architect then accepts a new client engagement for similar design work. What conflict analysis applies?

options.text: Expert witness work is completely separate and raises no conflicts, which is an oversimplification
The litigation position could bias advice to the new client; disclosure is required, and recusal may be necessary if the conflicts cannot be adequately mitigated
The architect must completely cease expert witness work if accepting any client design engagements, which is not always necessary
Confidential litigation information can be used to advise the new client as long as the architect doesn't mention the litigation, which is unethical

rationale.a: Litigation work in related areas creates conflicts through information flow and position bias.
rationale.c: Complete cessation is not required; disclosure and separation of engagement scopes can address the conflict.
rationale.d: Confidential information cannot be used in new engagements, even implicitly; the conflict often requires recusal.
rationale.correct: Litigation involvement creates professional and informational conflicts with new client work in the same domain; disclosure is required, and recusal may be necessary.
rationale.takeaway: Expert witness work on related matters creates conflicts requiring disclosure; recusal may be necessary if the two matters cannot be ethically separated.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Professional Conflicts & Recusal

questions.text: An architect's spouse owns an electrical contracting firm. The architect designs buildings and arranges for the spouse's firm to bid on electrical work without disclosing the family relationship to clients. What is the ethical violation?

options.text: Spousal involvement in construction is inherently prohibited, as it may lead to conflicts of interest
The architect's household financial interest in the spouse's selection, combined with non-disclosure, violates the duty of candor and creates appearance of divided loyalty
The spouse's firm must be prohibited from bidding on all projects, to prevent any potential bias or favoritism
The architect must recuse from all project involvement if a spouse works in construction, ensuring impartiality and fairness

rationale.a: Family involvement is permissible if disclosed and consented to; disclosure and consent cure the conflict.
rationale.c: Prohibition is not required; transparent disclosure and client consent allow the spouse's participation.
rationale.d: Recusal is not required; disclosure and client consent allow the architect to proceed while protecting the client's interests.
rationale.correct: Family financial interests create conflicts requiring disclosure; the architect has competing loyalty (household income from spouse's selection) that must be revealed and consent obtained.
rationale.takeaway: Family financial interests in contractors must be disclosed; without disclosure, the architect violates duties of candor and loyalty.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Family Financial Interests & Disclosure

questions.text: An architect frequently recommends the same structural engineer as subconsultant, in part due to friendship. The architect does not disclose the social relationship. What is the ethical issue and how is it resolved?

options.text: Friendships with consultants are professionally unethical and must be immediately terminated to prevent any bias
The friendship bias compromises the architect's judgment in selecting 'best-qualified' consultant; disclosure to clients and allowing competitive alternatives cures the conflict
Repeated recommendations to the same consultant are always prohibited, regardless of the consultant's qualifications
The architect's judgment about qualifications is personal and needs no disclosure, as long as the consultant meets minimum standards

rationale.a: Friendships are not inherently unethical; disclosure and transparency cure the conflict.
rationale.c: Repeat recommendations are acceptable if merit-based; the conflict is appearance, cured by disclosure.
rationale.d: Personal preference is exactly the problem; disclosure lets clients make informed decisions.
rationale.correct: Friendship creates appearance that recommendation is based on personal relationship, not merit; disclosure and competitive alternatives address the conflict.
rationale.takeaway: Friendship with subconsultants must be disclosed; clients should have the option to obtain competitive proposals.

questions.code_citation: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) / UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP 201-209) - Consultant Selection & Merit-Based Recommendation

questions.text: An architect is in a romantic relationship with a contractor bidding on the architect's project. The architect biases the recommendation toward the contractor without disclosure. What is the primary ethical problem?

options.text: Romantic relationships are permitted as long as the work is ultimately completed, which is the primary concern in professional settings
The non-disclosed personal relationship incentivizes biased recommendation away from client's objective selection process, violating the duty of loyalty and objectivity
The contractor must agree to the relationship before the architect can recommend their firm, ensuring mutual consent
Romantic relationships are only problematic if they are in a different profession, as this could lead to conflicts of interest

rationale.a: Completion doesn't cure the conflict; the client's selection process is compromised.
rationale.b: The contractor's knowledge doesn't change the architect's obligation to the client.
rationale.c: Professional background is irrelevant; any romantic relationship with a vendor creates conflict.
rationale.d: Best practice: recuse from recommendations involving romantic partners entirely.
rationale.correct: Undisclosed romantic relationships with vendors create conflicts where personal motivation biases professional recommendation, violating client loyalty.
rationale.takeaway: Romantic relationships with contractors or vendors require disclosure and typically warrant recusal from recommendation authority.
